description: DEF CON Groups talks from DEF CON 34.

talks.title: Building a Hacker Haven - The Long Game of Growing a Local Hacker Community
talks.teaser: Explains how two organizers turned a DEF CON 26 suggestion into a nonprofit hacker meetup, covering approvals, funding, boards, bylaws, and Code of Conduct issues.
talks.summary:
Two organizers recount how a suggestion at DEF CON 26 to start a local group became DC608 in Madison, Wisconsin. Their monthly meetup began with about three people and now draws roughly 45 to 50, supported by a Discord server and a nonprofit structure. They argue that in-person gatherings matter more after years of isolation, and that a group does not need a formal venue or polished speakers to begin.

Much of the talk is practical. They explain the approval process with DEF CON Groups, the cost of meetup listings, and how they moved from a community center with a strict closing time to an arcade bar and back to a donated, changing space. They describe fundraising through a low-fee donation platform, a visible tip jar, and the tactic of keeping some money showing so attendees feel encouraged to give. On governance, they cover Wisconsin's board requirements, recruiting around shared values, veto clauses in bylaws, regular board meetings, and enforcing a code of conduct evenly, including against board members. They also share how they recruited speakers by direct messages and ran lockpicking, Hack The Box, and Discord-based red and blue team nights.

The closing takeaways are to plan for growth, keep documentation current, and treat the community as a team effort rather than one organizer's job. They also say that paying a service to incorporate was not clearly worth it for them, and that a do-it-yourself filing may be cheaper.

talks.title: Building a Strong Community Culture presented by DC407
talks.teaser: Presents how the Orlando DEF CON group DC407 grows a welcoming community that moves members from attending to speaking, volunteering and leading.
talks.summary:
Two organizers from DC407, the DEF CON group in Orlando, open with the problem of turning passive attendees into active members. Their meetings are free and built around a talk or workshop, with socials, a sticker swap and a book swap. Students and mentors often send newcomers their way, but new people can feel like outsiders in an established crowd. The group answers this by greeting newcomers, introducing them to a few friendly members, and stating openly that the group is welcoming, with attention to microaggressions and a code of conduct that addresses harassment. Organizers suggested adapting that code to each venue's rules.

The middle of the talk covers growth. DC407 plans speaker slots two to three months ahead, sends written confirmations, runs a Discord with speaker roles, and offers short lightning talks on any subject so first-time presenters can start small. Members are encouraged to help set up events, volunteer with other local groups and B-Sides, and build a network of advisors so leaders do not carry everything alone. Consistency matters: a regular monthly cadence, steady online presence and word of mouth build the group slowly, even when few people show up.

The speakers also shared practical numbers. RSVPs typically convert to 40 to 60 percent actual attendance, a lesson they learned after overbuying pizza. They closed by describing the organizer's role as a facilitator who looks after a community that belongs to its members.

talks.title: Lessons Learned from Building a New DEF CON Group
talks.teaser: Explains how to launch a new DEF CON group, from checking for local competition and finding organizers to building partnerships and keeping members engaged.
talks.summary:
The session comes from the cofounders of DC724, a DEF CON group for the Greensburg, Pennsylvania area that formed after DEF CON 33 and had about 70 members at the time. They begin with the questions a prospective organizer should settle before applying: whether they have the time, whether a nearby group already exists that they could support instead, what the group should focus on, who will serve as point of contact, and where startup money will come from. Naming is covered too, with a city name as a fallback when area-code names are taken.

The middle of the talk covers the early months. The presenters describe the intake process through DEF CON's group leadership, the value of visiting an established group's meetings, and running in-person and virtual sessions with a consistent schedule. They recommend a Meetup page, a website, and Discord announcements. Feedback should be gathered through a mix of polls and direct conversation, used sparingly, and weighed for both praise and criticism. Delegation comes next: pick reliable people and let them own tasks they enjoy.

The closing section covers working with other local tech groups, which may decline, and planning for setbacks such as losing a meeting space, shifting partnerships, member turnover, and money structure. The takeaway is that a new group grows through relationships with other communities, shared contribution, and a backup plan for where people meet.

talks.title: The State of DEF CON Groups
talks.teaser: Walks through the DEF CON Groups department, the community's past year, and how anyone can start or join a local group.
talks.summary:
The DEF CON Groups department leads opened by describing the program: a network of more than 300 community-run local meetups across six continents, ranging from groups formed this year to ones that have met for two decades. They stressed that the meetups are free, open to everyone, and run by local organizers who shape their own culture. The speakers argued that these groups matter most between conferences, when attendees otherwise lose the peers they met in Las Vegas.

They then reviewed the past year. The department now has a leadership structure with regional leads and a team of eight, and it handles new group requests, point-of-contact changes, and code of conduct reports, escalating serious cases to conference safety staff. At the conference, the community ran a space with five stage talks, a party, the first official DEF CON contests (a sticker contest and a Backdoors and Breaches tournament), and collected 61 group applications and directory updates from more than 14 countries. Guidance covered starting a group with a single form and no ID check, naming groups after area codes, using the mascot in logos, accepting sponsor donations without profit or product pitches, and reserving "DEF CON" plus a city name for official events.

The session closed with calls for volunteers and organizers, followed by short stories from group leaders in western Pennsylvania, Orlando, and Kosovo. The main takeaway is that a group can begin with two people, and consistency over time matters more than size.

talks.title: Starting and Sustaining a Successful DEF CON Group presented by DC862
talks.teaser: Shows how DC862 founded and runs a DEF CON group, covering organizer roles, venues, speaker recruiting, outreach and succession planning.
talks.summary:
This panel, given by members of DC862 from New Jersey, opens with a reminder that a DEF CON group represents DEF CON, its members and each organizer personally, so conduct and branding matter. The group explains why it started: no DEF CON group existed in the area, and its founders wanted year-round events. Their advice for newcomers is to research existing groups nearby, write a simple mission statement, and begin with small, informal meetups at someone's home before growing.

The middle of the talk covers day-to-day operations. Applying for an official group name comes first, then a website and social channels, and Discord is used for onboarding, channel organization and sharing a code of conduct. Meetings need a consistent schedule, and hybrid streaming has helped draw in members from other states. Venues vary: the group tried several locations before finding one that welcomed them, and libraries and sponsor shops have also hosted meetings. Volunteer projects such as refurbishing donated laptops for schools and teaching older adults to spot scams help build the group's reputation. Swag and pizza are the main costs, and the speakers offset expenses with sponsorships and giveaways from Black Hat parties.

The closing section stresses sustainability. A leadership committee and shared ownership keep the group running when a founder moves or gets busy, and members are encouraged to lead their own sub-channels and give talks. Speakers are found by introducing interesting people met at other events to the organizer. The panel ends with homework: bring what you learned back to your local community.
